title: Jabr
def: A Christian craftsman of Mecca whom opponents claimed taught the Prophet, a charge the Quran answers.
what: Some Meccans said, “It is only a human being who teaches him.” The Quran replied: “The tongue of the one they point to is foreign, and this is a clear Arabic tongue” (16:103). The man named in reports, such as Jabr or Yasar, was a non-Arab who knew little Arabic, and could not have composed the Quran’s eloquence.
sources: Commentators gave several names for the man, and none is certain. The point stands: the Quran’s challenge for a surah like it (2:23) was met with silence, not a claim of a tutor.

title: Jacob
def: Son of Isaac and father of Joseph, a prophet whose patience in grief the Quran praises.
what: His birth was foretold with that of Isaac (11:71). “We gave him Isaac and Jacob, each of whom We guided” (6:84). He urged his sons to die as Muslims (2:132–133), and when Joseph was lost he said: “Beautiful patience!” (12:18). His other name was Israel (3:93).

title: Jadidism
def: A reform movement among Muslims of the Russian Empire in the late nineteenth century.
what: The Jadids, led by figures such as Ismail Gasprinski (1851–1914), set up “new method” schools that taught reading by sound, along with science, geography and languages, in place of rote learning only. They also printed newspapers and argued that Islam, rightly understood, calls for learning.

title: Jahiliyya
def: The “age of ignorance”: the Arabia before the Prophet, marked by idol worship, tribal feud and the burying of daughters.
what: The Quran uses the word for the pride and rage of the unbelievers (48:26) and warns women against “the display of the former jahiliyya” (33:33). Ja‘far ibn Abi Talib told the king of Abyssinia that before Islam “we were people of jahiliyya, worshipping idols, eating carrion, committing shameful acts, and the strong among us devoured the weak”, and that the Prophet called them to truth, honesty and kindness to kin (Musnad Ahmad). Poetry, hospitality and courage did exist then, and Islam kept the good.
misread: The word means a state of moral unawareness, not low intelligence, and some modern writers use it for any society that rejects divine guidance. It is a judgement on behaviour and not on a people.

title: Jamaat
def: A group or congregation, and the name of several Muslim movements.
what: The word means community, and the Prophet taught that “the hand of God is with the congregation” (al-Tirmidhi), and prayer in congregation is worth twenty-seven times prayer alone (Sahih al-Bukhari). Jamaat-e-Islami is a political and religious movement founded by Abul A‘la Maududi in 1941.

title: Jerusalem
def: The holy city of Jews, Christians and Muslims, whose Al-Aqsa Mosque was the first direction of Muslim prayer.
what: The Quran begins the Night Journey “from the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque, around which We have blessed” (17:1). The Prophet and the early Muslims prayed toward Jerusalem for about sixteen or seventeen months before the direction was changed to the Kaaba (2:142–144). He said that one prayer in Mecca’s mosque is worth more than in any other, and that travelling to pray is advised for three mosques only: Mecca, Medina and al-Aqsa (Sahih al-Bukhari). Umar entered Jerusalem in 637 and guaranteed its Christians safety for their churches.

title: Jews
def: The Quran honours Jews as People of the Book and descendants of the prophets, and it speaks of them in praise and in criticism.
what: “Those who believe, the Jews, the Christians and the Sabians, whoever believes in God and the Last Day and does good, shall have their reward with their Lord” (2:62; also 5:69). “Among the People of the Book are some who, if you trust them with a heap of gold, return it” (3:75). The Prophet stood up for the funeral procession of a Jew and said, “Is it not a soul?” (Sahih al-Bukhari). Jewish scholars flourished under Muslim rule, as Maimonides did in Cairo.
misread: The Quran’s criticisms address specific acts of some groups at the time of the revelation, and are paralleled by criticisms of Muslims; the Quran also speaks of the faithful among them (3:113–115). Hatred of Jews as a people has no basis in the Quran, and is rejected by mainstream scholars.

title: Jihad
def: Striving in the cause of God, which includes the moral struggle, and, under strict rules, defensive fighting.
what: The word means “striving”. The Quran commands Muslims to “strive for God as He deserves” (22:78) and, in an early Meccan verse, to strive against the unbelievers with the Quran itself (25:52). The word for armed fighting is a separate one, qitāl.

Permission to fight came after years of persecution, to “those who are fought, because they were wronged” (22:39). The same passage names monasteries, churches, synagogues and mosques as places that fighting is meant to protect (22:40).
misread: That jihad is holy war to convert or kill non-Muslims everywhere.
sources: The Quran limits fighting to those who fight, and forbids exceeding the limit (2:190). The Prophet is reported to have forbidden killing women and children (Sahih al-Bukhari), and Abu Bakr’s instructions to an army, recorded in the Muwatta of Malik, forbid killing the elderly, monks and non-combatants and cutting down fruit trees. A saying reported in Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi calls the best jihad “a word of truth before an unjust ruler”.

title: Jinn
def: Unseen beings made from smokeless fire, who like humans have free will and can believe or disbelieve.
what: “He created the jinn from a smokeless flame of fire” (55:15). Surah 72 is named for them: a group heard the Quran and said, “We have heard a wondrous recitation that guides to right conduct, and we believe in it” (72:1–2); some are righteous and some are not (72:11). Iblis was one of them (18:50). The Quran says that they and humans were created to worship God (51:56).
sources: Humans cannot see jinn, and only God knows the unseen (27:65). Scholars warn against fortune-telling and dealings with them (72:6), and affirm that no one is harmed except by God’s permission. The tales of genies in lamps are folklore.

title: Jizya
def: A tax paid by non-Muslim adult men under Muslim rule, in return for protection and exemption from military service.
what: The Quran mentions it once (9:29). In the classical law, women, children, the elderly, the poor and monks were exempt, and the tax was a due in place of the military service and the zakat that Muslims owed. In return the state owed protection of life, property and worship.
Abu Yusuf’s Kitab al-Kharaj reports that when Muslim forces in Syria could not protect a town, Abu Ubayda returned the tax they had collected, saying that without protection it was not owed.
misread: That it was a ransom or extortion, “convert or pay”.
sources: Treaties of the early period, such as that with the Christians of Najran, set a fixed sum and promise safety for their churches and clergy. The Quran’s phrase “while they are subdued” was read by some jurists, among them al-Shafi’i, as accepting the authority of the state’s law. Practice varied by time and ruler, and Muslims do not claim that every ruler honoured the ideal. Today the tax has no place in most states, where non-Muslims are citizens.

title: Job
def: A prophet who is held up as the model of patience in affliction.
what: “And Job, when he called to his Lord: ‘Harm has touched me, and You are the Most Merciful of the merciful.’ We answered him and removed the harm that was on him” (21:83–84). God calls him “an excellent servant, ever turning to Him” (38:44). The Quran gives no detail of the illness or of the loss; his story is the answer to hardship by patience and prayer.

title: John of Damascus
def: An eighth-century Christian theologian (d. around 749) who wrote one of the first Christian descriptions of Islam.
what: John of Damascus served in the early Umayyad court before becoming a monk, and he wrote of Islam as a Christian heresy in his work On Heresies. His text shows how Christians of the time first understood the new faith and which questions they raised: the nature of Christ, free will, and the Quran’s origin.
sources: Muslims answer that the Quran presents itself as a confirmation of the earlier prophets’ message and a correction of what was changed (5:48), not as a Christian sect. Scholars note that John’s picture of the Quran contains errors about its content.

title: Jonah
def: The prophet swallowed by a fish, who called out in the darkness and was saved; the tenth surah is named for him.
what: “And Dhu al-Nun, when he went off in anger, thinking We would not constrain him; then he cried out in the darknesses: ‘There is no god but You, glory be to You, I have been one of the wrongdoers.’ We answered him and saved him from distress” (21:87–88). He was sent to a hundred thousand or more (37:147), and they believed and were spared (10:98). The Prophet said not to prefer him over Jonah (Sahih al-Bukhari), a lesson of humility among prophets.
sources: The Quran says Jonah was cast on a bare shore while ill (37145), and God made a gourd tree grow over him; the supplication of 21:87 is a favourite of Muslims in distress.

title: Joseph
def: Son of Jacob, whose story, told in surah 12, the Quran calls “the best of stories”.
what: Surah 12 tells of his dream, the jealousy of his brothers, the well, slavery in Egypt, the false accusation, prison and rise to authority, and the reunion. It shows his patience, his chastity, and his forgiveness: “No blame on you today; may God forgive you” (12:92). Jacob’s answer to his grief is “beautiful patience” (12:18, 12:83).

title: Judgement
def: Judgement in the Quran: God’s judgement on the Last Day, and the duty to judge with justice among people.
what: “God commands you to render trusts to their owners, and when you judge between people, to judge with justice” (4:58). “Do not let hatred of a people prevent you from being just; be just, that is closer to piety” (5:8). The Quran repeats that every person will be shown his record, and none will be wronged “by even the weight of an atom” (4:40, 99:7–8).

title: Judi
def: The mountain on which the Quran says Noah’s ark came to rest.
what: “It was said: ‘O earth, swallow your water, and O sky, withhold’; the water subsided, the matter was decided, and the ship came to rest on al-Judi” (11:44). The Quran names no site on the map, and the name Judi is applied by tradition to a mountain in the Kurdish region of the upper Tigris.

title: Junayd al-Baghdadi
def: A Baghdad scholar and Sufi (d. 910) known as “the master of the group”, who kept the Sufi path in line with the law.
what: Junayd taught that the path of Sufism is bound by the Quran and the Sunna, and held that sobriety, with strict adherence to law, is a higher state than the ecstasy of those who lose themselves. He was a jurist of the school of Abu Thawr, and his letters and sayings are studied across Sufi orders.

title: Justice
def: Fair dealing: the Quran commands justice even toward those one dislikes.
what: “God commands justice and excellence” (16:90). “O you who believe, be steadfast for God, witnesses in fairness, and do not let hatred of a people prevent you from being just; be just, that is closer to piety” (5:8). “Stand firm for justice, as witnesses for God, even against yourselves, your parents and relatives” (4:135). Al-‘Adl, the Just, is one of God’s names.
